modules.title: The accounting equation
modules.summary: See what a business owns, what it owes and what belongs to its owner.

sections.title: Start with the business, not its owner
sections.text: An entity keeps records separately from its owner. An asset is a resource controlled by the entity, such as bank funds, equipment or money owed by customers. A liability is an obligation, such as a loan or an unpaid supplier.
sections.new: Imagine a separate box labelled 'the business'. Only things belonging to that box go in its accounts. Your personal shopping is not a business expense.

sections.title: Everything has a funding story
sections.text: Assets = liabilities + equity. Your notes call equity 'ownership interest'. Equity is the residual interest after liabilities are deducted. Capital contributions increase it; drawings or dividends reduce it. Profit increases equity and a loss reduces it.
sections.new: If the business has £900 and owes £300, the owner's share is the remaining £600. Equity is a claim on net assets, not a separate pile of cash.

sections.title: Transactions keep the equation balanced
sections.text: Taking a loan increases both bank and liabilities. Buying equipment with bank funds swaps one asset for another. Earning revenue increases equity through profit; paying an expense reduces equity through profit. A transaction can affect two assets without changing total assets.
sections.new: Think 'what changed?' and then 'what is the other side?' The equation must still balance after every transaction.

example.prompt: A new business receives £5,000 from its owner, borrows £2,000 and buys equipment for £1,500 from its bank account.
steps: Owner contribution: bank £5,000; capital £5,000.
Loan: bank rises to £7,000; loan liability £2,000.
Equipment purchase: bank falls to £5,500; equipment becomes £1,500.
Assets £7,000 = liabilities £2,000 + equity £5,000.
example.result: Buying the equipment changes the mix of assets, not total equity.

modules.watch: Cash received is not always income. Owner capital and loan proceeds are not sales.

terms.definition: The residual interest in assets after deducting liabilities.
An amount a customer owes the business for a credit sale.

reading.topics: Accounting equation; assets, liabilities and capital

questions.q: A business has assets of £12,000 and liabilities of £4,500. What is equity?
questions.explain: Equity is assets less liabilities: £12,000 − £4,500 = £7,500.
questions.hint: Rearrange assets = liabilities + equity.

questions.q: Which item is a liability?
questions.explain: The supplier must be paid: this is a trade payable. A customer owing the business is an asset.
questions.hint: Look for something the business owes, not something owed to it.

questions.q: The owner pays £2,000 of personal savings into the business. What changes?
questions.explain: The owner provides capital. Bank is an asset and capital is equity; this is not revenue.
questions.hint: The owner is funding the business, not buying its products.

questions.q: Equipment costing £800 is bought using bank funds. What happens to total assets immediately?
questions.explain: Equipment increases £800 while bank decreases £800. It is an asset swap.
questions.hint: Count both the new equipment and the reduction in bank.

questions.q: The business receives a £3,000 bank loan. Which is correct?
questions.explain: Bank increases and a repayment obligation is created. Borrowing does not create profit.
questions.hint: Does the cash have to be repaid?

questions.q: Which transaction normally reduces equity without being an expense?
questions.explain: Drawings are a withdrawal by the owner, not a cost of earning business revenue.
questions.hint: Separate the owner's withdrawals from running costs.

questions.q: Assets are £20,000 and liabilities are £8,000. The owner withdraws £1,000 cash. What is the new equity?
questions.explain: Opening equity is £12,000. Drawings reduce bank and equity by £1,000, leaving £11,000.
questions.hint: Calculate equity first, then deduct drawings.

questions.q: A business pays £600 of an existing supplier debt from bank. What changes?
questions.explain: Bank decreases and the payable decreases. The expense or purchase was recognised earlier.
questions.hint: Settling a liability is not recording a new purchase.

modules.title: Debits & credits, without the guesswork
modules.summary: Use account types to choose the right side of every entry.

sections.title: Left and right, not good and bad
sections.text: Debit (Dr) means the left side of an account; credit (Cr) means the right. Every transaction has equal total debits and credits. Neither word alone means an increase, a decrease, money in or money out.
sections.new: Debit and credit are directions, like left and right. First identify the account type; only then decide which side changes it.

sections.title: Learn the increase sides
sections.text: Assets and expenses increase with debits. Liabilities, equity and income increase with credits. Decreases go on the opposite side. Drawings are normally a debit because they reduce the owner's equity. Accumulated depreciation is a contra-asset with a normal credit balance.
sections.new: A useful pair: assets and expenses grow on the left. Liabilities, capital and income grow on the right. Reverse the side when something shrinks.

sections.title: Use a three-step routine
sections.text: Name the affected accounts. Decide whether each increases or decreases. Apply the debit/credit rule and check that total debits equal total credits. For a multi-line journal, there may be more than one debit or credit.
sections.new: Do not try to memorise every possible transaction. Work out the accounts and their changes, one at a time.

example.prompt: Pay £240 rent from the business bank account.
steps: Rent is an expense and increases: debit Rent £240.
Bank is an asset and decreases: credit Bank £240.
The journal has a £240 debit and £240 credit.

modules.watch: Your bank statement is written from the bank's perspective. Use the business's perspective in its own ledger.

terms.definition: A dated record of debit and credit entries, usually with a short explanation.
An account with the opposite normal balance to an asset, used to reduce its carrying amount.

reading.topics: Double entry; income and expenses; the journal

questions.q: An asset increases. Which entry is normally needed?
options: Both sides of the same account
questions.explain: Assets increase on the debit side and decrease on the credit side.
questions.hint: Assets and expenses share the same increase side.

questions.q: A liability increases. Which side records the increase?
questions.explain: Liabilities increase with credits. A debit would reduce the liability.
questions.hint: Liabilities, equity and income have the same normal increase side.

questions.q: Pay £90 electricity from bank. Which journal is correct?
questions.explain: Electricity expense increases (debit) and bank decreases (credit). Both entries are £90.
questions.hint: Identify the expense increasing and the asset decreasing.

questions.q: What does 'credit' mean on its own?
options: The right-hand side of an account
questions.explain: Credit is a side, not a universal increase or decrease. Its effect depends on account type.
questions.hint: Think position rather than economic meaning.

questions.q: Sales revenue increases by £700. What happens in the sales account?
questions.explain: Income increases with a credit. The other entry is to bank or trade receivables.
questions.hint: Revenue increases equity through profit.

questions.q: A journal has debits of £300 and £50. What must total credits equal?
questions.explain: Add the debit lines: £350. Double entry requires equal total credits, not necessarily equal numbers of lines.
questions.hint: Balance totals, not the number of entries.

questions.q: Which account normally has a credit balance?
questions.explain: Accumulated depreciation is a contra-asset. Its credit balance offsets the asset's debit cost balance.
questions.hint: One choice reduces the carrying amount of another asset account.

questions.q: A supplier liability falls by £500. How is that liability account affected?
questions.explain: A liability's normal balance is credit, so a debit reduces it. Payment would also credit bank £500.
questions.hint: A decrease uses the opposite side from an increase.

modules.title: Purchases & paying suppliers
modules.summary: Distinguish resale goods, assets and expenses, then follow a supplier payment.

sections.title: What did the business actually buy?
sections.text: Trading businesses buy goods for resale. In these periodic-inventory exercises, record them in Purchases. Equipment used over several periods is a non-current asset. Rent and utilities are expenses. The word 'purchase' in everyday speech does not mean every item belongs in Purchases.
sections.new: A cafe buying cakes to sell records purchases. Buying its oven records equipment. Paying to keep the lights on records an electricity expense.

sections.title: Cash now or a promise to pay?
sections.text: A cash purchase of resale goods is Dr Purchases, Cr Bank. A credit purchase is Dr Purchases, Cr Trade payables. Credit purchases create a liability because the supplier has not yet been paid. Use the relevant asset or expense instead of Purchases for other kinds of item.
sections.new: Ask whether money left the bank today. If not, the supplier is waiting for payment: that waiting amount is a payable.

sections.title: Settlement is a different event
sections.text: Later payment is Dr Trade payables, Cr Bank. It reduces both the liability and bank. Do not record the purchases again. We ignore VAT and discounts throughout unless an exercise says otherwise.
sections.new: The invoice records what was bought. The payment clears what is owed. Recording purchases at both stages would count the goods twice.

example.prompt: Buy £900 of goods for resale on credit. Later pay £650 of that invoice.
steps: Invoice: Dr Purchases £900; Cr Trade payables £900.
Payment: Dr Trade payables £650; Cr Bank £650.
Remaining supplier liability: £900 − £650 = £250.
example.result: Purchases remain £900; trade payables have a £250 credit balance.

modules.watch: Periodic and perpetual inventory systems use different inventory entries. The questions here explicitly use the periodic purchases account convention.

terms.definition: An amount owed to a supplier for goods or services received on credit.
Expenditure recognised as an asset rather than an immediate running expense.

reading.topics: Purchases of inventory; capital versus revenue expenditure; credit purchases

questions.q: Under a periodic system, buy £400 of goods for resale on credit. Which journal?
questions.explain: Purchases increases by debit and the supplier liability increases by credit, both £400.
questions.hint: No cash moves today; a supplier is owed money.

questions.q: Buy a computer for long-term business use for £800 from bank. What is debited?
questions.explain: The computer is an asset used in the business, not inventory held for resale.
questions.hint: Will the business sell it as stock or use it to operate?

questions.q: Pay £300 of an existing supplier balance. Which journal?
questions.explain: Debit the liability to reduce it; credit bank to reduce the asset.
questions.hint: The purchase was recorded when the invoice arrived.

questions.q: Why should a supplier settlement not be debited to Purchases again?
options: It would count the purchase twice
questions.explain: The invoice already recorded the purchase. Settlement clears the payable, not a new purchase.
questions.hint: Distinguish receiving goods from paying for them.

questions.q: Opening trade payables are £1,200. New credit purchases are £800 and payments are £900. Closing payables?
questions.hint: Add what becomes owed and subtract what is settled.

questions.q: Which item belongs in Purchases in these trading exercises?
questions.explain: Purchases is used for resale inventory here. Rent is an expense; the van is a non-current asset.
questions.hint: Look for goods destined for customers.

questions.q: An unpaid £200 electricity bill is recorded. What is the effect?
questions.explain: The electricity expense increases, and the supplier liability increases. No bank entry occurs until payment.
questions.hint: A service can create a payable too, but is not resale inventory.

questions.q: Equipment £1,500 is bought with £500 paid now and £1,000 due later. Which entry is correct?
options: Dr Equipment £1,500; Cr Bank £500; Cr Payables £1,000
questions.explain: Recognise the full asset cost. Funding is split between bank and a liability; credits total £1,500.
questions.hint: The asset is received in full even though payment is split.

modules.title: Sales & collecting from customers
modules.summary: Follow cash sales, credit sales and customer receipts without double-counting income.

sections.title: Recognise the sale
sections.text: In these simple goods-sale examples, recognise revenue when the goods are supplied to the customer. A cash sale is Dr Bank, Cr Sales. A credit sale is Dr Trade receivables, Cr Sales. The receivable is an asset: a right to collect from the customer.
sections.new: You can earn a sale before money reaches the bank. A receivable is the business's 'customer owes us' record.

sections.title: Collecting is not another sale
sections.text: When a credit customer pays, record Dr Bank, Cr Trade receivables. One asset becomes another. Revenue was already recognised at the sale, so do not credit Sales a second time.
sections.new: Move the amount from 'owed to us' into 'in our bank'. The customer has not bought the same item again.

sections.title: Sales are not profit
sections.text: Revenue is the selling amount. Profit also considers the costs of earning it. Under a periodic inventory system, the cost of goods sold is calculated at period end rather than necessarily journalled at each sale. A cash receipt before supply can be a liability, covered in Unit 3.
sections.new: Selling something for £100 does not mean £100 profit. If it cost £60, the gross profit is £40.

example.prompt: Sell goods for £1,200 on credit. The customer later pays £750.
steps: Sale: Dr Trade receivables £1,200; Cr Sales £1,200.
Receipt: Dr Bank £750; Cr Trade receivables £750.
Outstanding receivable: £1,200 − £750 = £450.

modules.watch: A debit balance in trade receivables normally means customers owe the business. It is not the business's supplier debt.

terms.definition: Income from the entity's ordinary activities, such as sales.
A sale for which the customer will pay later.

questions.q: Sell goods for £600 cash, deposited into bank. Which journal records revenue?
questions.explain: Bank increases by debit and sales revenue increases by credit, both £600.
questions.hint: Identify the asset received and the income earned.

questions.q: Sell £900 of goods on credit. Which account is debited?
questions.explain: The customer owes £900: increase the receivable asset with a debit.
questions.hint: No money has arrived yet, but the business has a right to receive it.

questions.q: A customer pays an existing £250 debt. Which account is credited?
questions.explain: Credit trade receivables to reduce the customer's debt; debit bank £250.
questions.hint: The receipt clears an asset that was created at the sale.

questions.q: Credit sales are £1,000 and £700 is collected. Ignoring opening balances, closing receivables are:
questions.explain: Customers still owe £1,000 − £700 = £300.
questions.hint: Start with amounts owed, then subtract collections.

questions.q: Which statement is correct about a credit sale and its later receipt?
options: Revenue is recorded at the sale, not again at collection
questions.explain: Collection swaps receivables for bank. It does not create new sales.
questions.hint: Ask when the goods were supplied.

questions.q: A trade receivable is normally classified as:
questions.explain: It is a right to receive money from a customer, so it is an asset.
questions.hint: Who owes whom?

questions.q: Opening receivables £500; credit sales £1,800; collections £1,650. Closing receivables?
questions.explain: £500 + £1,800 − £1,650 = £650. Include the opening customer debts.
questions.hint: Opening balance + new credit sales − receipts.

questions.q: Cash sales £400, credit sales £900, receipts from old customer debts £300. What is sales revenue?
questions.explain: Revenue is £400 + £900 = £1,300. Collecting old debts is not current sales.
questions.hint: Exclude collections relating to sales already recorded.

modules.title: Capital, loans & investments
modules.summary: Tell funding received apart from money lent or invested by the business.

sections.title: Money coming into the business
sections.text: Owner funding is Dr Bank, Cr Capital. Borrowed funds are Dr Bank, Cr Loan payable. Both increase bank, but capital is equity and the loan is a liability. Repaying loan principal is Dr Loan payable, Cr Bank; principal repayment is not an expense.
sections.new: Two people give the business money. An owner takes the risk of ownership; a lender expects repayment. Same cash movement, different funding story.

sections.title: Money going out as an investment or loan
sections.text: If the business lends to someone else: Dr Loan receivable, Cr Bank. Buying an investment is Dr Investment, Cr Bank. Both create assets rather than immediate expenses. Recovering principal is Dr Bank, Cr Loan receivable; selling an investment may also create a gain or loss.
sections.new: An outgoing loan is something owed to the business. An incoming loan is something owed by the business. Always label whose loan it is.

sections.title: Separate principal from returns
sections.text: Interest received and dividend income are returns on funds invested, not recovery of the original principal. A simple receipt is Dr Bank, Cr Interest income or Dividend income. Interest on the business's own borrowing is an expense. Returns of principal reduce the relevant loan or investment balance.
sections.new: Principal is the original pot of money. Interest is the price of using it. Keep those two parts in separate accounts.

example.prompt: The business lends £2,000 to another entity and later receives £2,100: £2,000 principal plus £100 interest.
steps: Set-up: Dr Loan receivable £2,000; Cr Bank £2,000.
Receipt: Dr Bank £2,100; Cr Loan receivable £2,000; Cr Interest income £100.
Only £100 is income. The loan receivable is now nil.
example.result: Getting your own principal back is not earning it again.

modules.watch: Use explicit labels such as 'loan payable' and 'loan receivable'. 'Loan' alone can hide which side of the transaction you are on.

terms.definition: The amount borrowed or lent, excluding interest.
An asset held to earn returns or increase in value.

reading.topics: Capital versus liabilities; income; introduction to company finance (related reading)

questions.q: Receive a new £5,000 loan from a bank. Which journal?
questions.explain: Bank increases and the obligation to repay increases; no income is earned.
questions.hint: Borrowing creates a liability.

questions.q: Lend £800 to another business. Which account is debited?
questions.explain: The business now has a right to recover £800, an asset called a loan receivable.
questions.hint: This business is the lender, not the borrower.

questions.q: Repay £500 of loan principal from bank. What is debited?
questions.explain: Debit the loan liability to reduce it; credit bank. Principal repayment does not reduce profit.
questions.hint: Reduce what the business owes.

questions.q: Receive £60 interest on a loan made to another entity. Which journal?
questions.explain: The interest is earned income, distinct from recovery of principal.
questions.hint: The business has earned a return for lending.

questions.q: The owner contributes £1,000. Why is it not sales revenue?
options: It is funding from the owner, not earned from customers
questions.explain: Capital contributions increase equity directly; they are not trading income.
questions.hint: Distinguish funding a business from buying from it.

questions.q: Buy an investment for £1,400 from bank. Immediate effect on total assets?
questions.explain: Bank decreases and the investment asset increases by the same amount.
questions.hint: One asset is exchanged for another.

questions.q: Receive £1,030: £1,000 recovery of a loan made and £30 interest. What is credited?
questions.explain: The receipt removes the £1,000 asset and recognises only £30 as income; debit bank £1,030.
questions.hint: Split principal recovery from the return earned.

questions.q: A £4,000 loan payable is reduced by a £600 principal payment. What is the closing liability and profit effect?
questions.explain: Principal falls to £3,400. Interest, if any, would be accounted for separately as an expense.
questions.hint: Principal repayment changes the balance sheet, not profit.

modules.title: Drawings, dividends & grants
modules.summary: Not every cash payment is an expense, and not every receipt is income.

sections.title: Withdrawals and distributions
sections.text: A sole trader's drawings are Dr Drawings, Cr Bank. They reduce equity, not profit. Dividends paid by a company are also distributions of equity, not expenses. For an immediately paid dividend in these simplified examples, debit Dividends (equity distribution) and credit Bank; a previously declared unpaid dividend involves a payable.
sections.new: The owner taking money home is not a cost of running the business. Keep owner transactions separate from wages, rent and interest.

sections.title: Expenses and gifts paid out
sections.text: Loan interest is a finance expense: Dr Interest expense, Cr Bank when paid. A straightforward charitable grant or donation paid with nothing directly in return is Dr Grants paid expense, Cr Bank. Do not confuse an expense grant paid out with owner drawings.
sections.new: Ask why the cash left. Paying for borrowed funds is a business cost. Giving money to a charity can be an expense. Giving money back to owners is different.

sections.title: Grants received need conditions checked
sections.text: A grant is not automatically recognised as income on receipt. Under the assumed deferral approach, cash for future costs is Dr Bank, Cr Deferred grant income, then released to income as related costs arise. An unconditional grant relating wholly to current costs may be current income under the exercise's assumptions.
sections.new: Receiving money with future obligations can mean 'we still owe performance'. Check what the grant requires before calling it earned income.

example.prompt: A sole trader withdraws £200, pays loan interest £40 and gives £60 to charity, all from bank.
steps: Drawings: Dr Drawings £200; Cr Bank £200.
Interest: Dr Interest expense £40; Cr Bank £40.
Donation: Dr Grants paid expense £60; Cr Bank £60.
Bank falls £300. Expenses reduce profit by £100; drawings do not affect profit.
example.result: Cash out £300 is not the same as expenses £300.

modules.watch: The lecture shorthand 'dividend expense' should not be used to treat dividends paid as an income statement expense.

terms.definition: A sole trader's withdrawal of business resources for personal use.
A transfer of equity to owners, such as a company dividend.

reading.topics: Drawings; income and expenses; company equity and distributions. Grant details: use lecture notes and your book index.

questions.q: The owner withdraws £120 cash for personal use. What is debited?
questions.explain: Personal withdrawals reduce equity through drawings. They are not wages or business expenses.
questions.hint: This is an owner transaction, not a running cost.

questions.q: A dividend paid to shareholders is normally:
questions.explain: Dividends are distributions to owners and do not reduce the company's profit as expenses.
questions.hint: Shareholders receive a distribution in their capacity as owners.

questions.q: Pay £75 interest on a business loan. Which journal?
questions.explain: Interest is the cost of borrowing; bank decreases. This is separate from loan principal repayment.
questions.hint: The payment is for using borrowed funds, not returning principal.

questions.q: Pay a £300 charitable grant with nothing directly in return. Which account is debited?
questions.explain: The straightforward donation is recognised as an expense, with a credit to bank.
questions.hint: It is neither an owner withdrawal nor the purchase of an asset.

questions.q: A grant is received for next year's costs, using the deferral approach. What is credited on receipt?
questions.explain: The cash is not yet recognised as earned income under these assumptions. Deferred grant income is a liability.
questions.hint: Cash arrives before the related costs and earning conditions.

questions.q: Which payment directly reduces profit?
questions.explain: Interest is an expense. Principal repayment, drawings and acquisition of an asset are not themselves current expenses.
questions.hint: Look for a cost of using finance.

questions.q: Bank falls £700: drawings £400, interest £100, donation £200. How much reduces profit?
questions.explain: Interest £100 plus donation expense £200 = £300. Drawings reduce equity separately.
questions.hint: Exclude the owner's withdrawal from expenses.

questions.q: A company pays an already-recorded dividend payable of £500. Which journal?
questions.explain: The payment clears the existing dividend liability. It is not a new expense or a second distribution entry.
questions.hint: An existing payable must be reduced.

modules.title: Inventory, cost of sales & gross profit
modules.summary: Connect goods bought, goods left and the cost of the goods actually sold.

sections.title: Trading versus manufacturing
sections.text: A trading business buys goods to resell. A manufacturer converts raw materials into finished goods. Manufacturing inventory can include raw materials, work in progress and finished goods. Inventory remaining at the reporting date is an asset, not all a current-period cost of sales.
sections.new: A shop resells a finished mug. A pottery business makes one. Both may hold inventory, but a maker can also hold clay and half-finished mugs.

sections.title: Match the cost to the units sold
sections.text: If every unit has the same cost, cost of sales = units sold × unit cost. Closing inventory = units still held × unit cost. With changing purchase prices, the FIFO or AVCO method determines which costs go to sales and which remain in inventory.
sections.new: Split the goods into 'sold' and 'still on the shelf'. The cost of the sold pile is an expense; the other pile is an asset.

sections.title: Calculate gross profit
sections.text: Under a simple periodic system, cost of sales = opening inventory + purchases − closing inventory. Gross profit = sales − cost of sales. Operating expenses, such as rent, are deducted after gross profit to reach a further profit subtotal. Ignore carriage, returns and VAT unless given.
sections.new: Sales minus the cost of what you sold gives gross profit. It is not the final profit because other business costs still need to come off.

example.prompt: Buy 100 identical items at £8 each. Sell 70 at £12 each. There is no opening inventory.
steps: Cost of sales: 70 × £8 = £560.
Closing inventory: 30 × £8 = £240.
Gross profit: £840 − £560 = £280. Check £800 purchases = £560 sold + £240 left.
example.result: Inventory is valued at cost in this example, not at the selling price.

modules.watch: Inventory may need a write-down to net realisable value. Unit 3 introduces the lower-of-cost-and-NRV rule.

terms.definition: Sales revenue less cost of sales.
Partly completed goods held by a manufacturer.

reading.topics: Inventory purchases; income statements; inventory valuation

questions.q: A trader buys 50 units at £6 each and sells 35. What is closing inventory at cost?
questions.explain: 15 units remain; 15 × £6 = £90.
questions.hint: Find units left before multiplying by cost.

questions.q: Sales are £2,400 and cost of sales £1,500. Gross profit is:
questions.explain: Gross profit = sales − cost of sales = £900.
questions.hint: Gross profit is the margin after the cost of goods sold.

questions.q: Opening inventory £300, purchases £1,200, closing inventory £400. Cost of sales?
questions.explain: £300 + £1,200 − £400 = £1,100. Goods left are not treated as sold.
questions.hint: Start with goods available at cost, then remove the goods still held.

questions.q: Which describes manufacturing?
options: Buying finished goods only to resell
Converting raw materials into finished goods
questions.explain: Manufacturing transforms materials; trading normally resells goods without that production process.
questions.hint: Look for production rather than resale.

questions.q: Which inventory category is partly finished production?
questions.explain: Work in progress is the cost of goods that have entered production but are not yet finished.
questions.hint: The goods are between raw materials and finished goods.

questions.q: 40 units costing £5 each are sold for £9 each. Gross profit?
questions.explain: Revenue £360 − cost £200 = gross profit £160, or 40 × £4 margin.
questions.hint: Use selling price minus cost per unit, then multiply by units sold.

questions.q: Sales £5,000; opening inventory £700; purchases £2,800; closing inventory £900; rent £400. Gross profit?
questions.explain: Cost of sales is £700 + £2,800 − £900 = £2,600. Gross profit £2,400; rent is deducted afterwards.
questions.hint: Do not deduct rent in the gross profit calculation.

questions.q: Closing inventory is accidentally overstated by £200. What happens to gross profit?
questions.explain: Too much closing inventory is subtracted from cost of sales, understating cost of sales and overstating gross profit by £200.
questions.hint: Follow the minus closing inventory term through the formula.

modules.title: Ledgers, trial balances & presentation
modules.summary: Turn entries into running balances and a trial balance, then interpret what they can tell you.

sections.title: Build a running-balance ledger
sections.text: Each account has a title and columns for date, description, reference, debit, credit and balance. A running balance updates after every entry. Treat debits as positive and credits as negative when calculating, then display the absolute amount with Dr or Cr. An overdrawn bank may have a credit balance.
sections.new: A ledger is one account's story. Start at its old balance, add its debits and subtract its credits. The sign tells you which side the closing balance sits on.

sections.title: Extract a trial balance
sections.text: List each ledger's closing balance once in either the debit or credit column. Do not list the total movements instead. Total debits should equal total credits. Assets, expenses and drawings normally appear as debits; liabilities, equity, income and accumulated depreciation normally appear as credits.
sections.new: The trial balance is a snapshot of all the account balances, not a second list of every transaction.

sections.title: Agreement is a check, not a guarantee
sections.text: A trial balance can agree despite complete omissions, entries in the wrong accounts or equal offsetting errors. Financial statements can look different because of IFRS versus UK GAAP, entity size, local requirements, terminology or order. 'Balance sheet' and 'statement of financial position' refer to the same statement.
sections.new: If both sides of a wrong entry are equal, the arithmetic still balances. A tidy total is useful evidence, not proof that every account is correct.

example.prompt: Bank starts at £1,000 Dr. Receive £500 owner capital and pay £200 rent. All other accounts start at zero.
steps: Opening capital was £1,000 Cr; the contribution makes capital £1,500 Cr.
Rent expense is £200 Dr.
Trial balance: debits £1,300 + £200 = £1,500; credits £1,500.
example.result: List the bank's £1,300 closing balance, not its £1,500 receipts total.

modules.watch: Normal balances are a guide, not a rule that overrides the actual ledger balance. An overdraft is a bank credit balance.

terms.definition: A list of ledger closing balances used to check equality of total debits and credits.
Statement of financial position, also called the balance sheet.

reading.topics: Balancing ledgers; trial balance; balance sheets; reporting concepts; undetected errors

questions.q: Bank starts £400 Dr. Record debit £250 and credit £100. Closing balance?
questions.hint: Add debits and subtract credits from a debit opening balance.

questions.q: What goes into a trial balance for each account?
options: The closing balance on its Dr or Cr side
questions.explain: The trial balance lists closing balances, not gross transaction totals.
questions.hint: It is a snapshot after the ledger has been balanced.

questions.q: Which balance normally belongs in the credit column?
questions.explain: Trade payables are liabilities, normally with credit balances.
questions.hint: Look for an obligation rather than a resource or cost.

questions.q: Which error can leave a trial balance agreeing?
options: Omitting both sides of a £100 transaction
questions.explain: A complete omission affects neither total; agreement cannot detect it.
questions.hint: An error affecting both sides equally can hide.

questions.q: Which is another name for a balance sheet?
questions.explain: Balance sheet and statement of financial position are alternative names for the statement of assets, liabilities and equity.
questions.hint: Think of the statement reporting the entity at a date.

questions.q: Why might two entities' financial statements have different layouts?
options: Standards, size and terminology can differ
Only one entity can make a profit
A trial balance cannot be used
questions.explain: Applicable IFRS or UK GAAP rules, size-related requirements and presentation choices can affect layout.
questions.hint: Presentation can differ while underlying accounting principles remain.

questions.q: Bank opens £200 Dr and payments of £350 are recorded, with no receipts. Closing bank?
questions.explain: £200 − £350 = −£150: an overdraft, displayed £150 Cr.
questions.hint: A negative debit-based balance is shown as a credit.

questions.q: Equipment bought for £600 is wrongly debited to Rent, with Bank correctly credited. Which is true?
options: Trial balance agrees but expenses are overstated
questions.explain: Equal debit and credit totals still agree. Rent is overstated and equipment understated, reducing profit incorrectly.
questions.hint: The sides balance even though the debit account is wrong.
